golden-hour-length.caption:
Golden hour is rarely an hour

It depends where you are
Near the equator the sun climbs steeply, so the warm, low light can be over in 20 minutes or so. In Scotland in winter the sun stays low all day, and on summer evenings the glow can run on for hours.

What to do about it
• Look up sunrise and sunset for the exact place, not your home town
• Arrive 45 minutes early and be set up before the light arrives
• Stay 20 minutes after the sun goes for the afterglow and blue hour

What is your favourite time of day to shoot, and why? Tell me in the comments.

calm-behind-the-camera.caption:
The calm behind the camera

In the flow
I go out for the experience: being in the moment, in the flow, where time gets lost and the noise of everyday life is shut out. I speak from experience when I say it calms me.

Why it works
• Looking for a photograph keeps your attention on what is in front of you, not on what is in your head
• Flow, being completely absorbed in what you are doing, tends to come when the challenge matches your skill
• A large study in England linked at least two hours a week in nature with better health and wellbeing

Try it next time
• Put your phone on silent and leave it in your pocket
• Spend five minutes just looking before you take a photograph
• Notice the sounds, the air and how the light moves
• Go slowly: one place, one hour, a handful of frames

Does photography calm you too? What does being out with a camera do for you? Tell me in the comments.

You need an expensive camera

The truth
Light, timing and composition do most of the work. This photograph of Lindisfarne was taken on a Canon 600D, an entry-level camera from 2011.

• Very low light, where bigger sensors stay cleaner
• Fast action, where focus speed counts

level-horizons.caption:
Straighten the sea

Why it matters
A sloping sea looks like a mistake, because everyone knows water lies flat. Even one degree out is noticeable.

In the camera
• Turn on the electronic level in the viewfinder or screen
• Turn on a grid and line the horizon up with it
• On a tripod, level the head, not just the legs

Afterwards
Use the straighten tool in your editor’s crop. Draw along the horizon and it rotates for you. You lose a little from the edges, so leave some room when you shoot.

raw-or-jpeg.caption:
RAW or JPEG?

The case for RAW
• Far more room to recover highlights and shadows
• White balance can be changed freely later
• Nothing is thrown away by the camera

The case for JPEG
• Ready to share straight away
• Much smaller files
• The camera’s colour and sharpening are often very good

A middle way
Most cameras can save both. Use the JPEG when it is right and the RAW when you need to fix something.

Which do you shoot, and has the other one ever saved you? Tell me in the comments.

cold-weather-care.caption:
Cold camera, warm room

The problem
Bring a cold camera into a warm room and moisture condenses on the lens and inside the body, just like a cold glass in summer.

The fix
• Before you go inside, seal the camera in a plastic bag or close it in your camera bag
• Let it warm up slowly for an hour or two before opening
• Take the card out first if you want to start editing

And outside
Batteries lose charge quickly in the cold. Carry spares in an inside pocket, and swap them as the one in the camera fades.

guide-lindisfarne.caption:
Photographing Lindisfarne

Plan around the tide
Holy Island is cut off by the sea twice a day. Check Northumberland County Council’s safe crossing times for your date, allow an extra 30 minutes, and never drive onto the causeway when it is closed.

What to look for
• The castle on its crag, from the harbour and the shore
• The old boat sheds near the harbour
• The priory ruins in the village
• The causeway itself as the water comes and goes

Make the most of it
• Stay through high tide, when the day visitors have gone and the island is quiet
• Bring a longer lens for the castle from across the harbour
• Walking routes across the sands need daylight and local knowledge

thirds-myth.caption:
Always use the rule of thirds

The truth
The rule of thirds is a good habit, not a law. It stops everything landing in the middle by default.

When to break it
• Symmetry and reflections, where the centre is the point
• A small subject in a lot of space, pushed right to the edge
• Patterns that fill the whole frame

The real rule
Put things where you mean them to be. If you can say why the subject sits there, it is probably right.

Rule follower or rule breaker? Tell me in the comments.

What a leading line is
Anything that carries the eye through the frame: a road, a wall, a railing, a shoreline, a row of lights.

Making them work

• Make sure it leads to something worth arriving at
• Get low or wide to make the line stronger
• Watch that it does not lead the eye straight out of the frame

nd-filter-maths.caption:
ND filters without the maths headache

Each stop doubles the time
• 3 stops: 1/125 s becomes 1/15 s
• 6 stops: 1/125 s becomes 1/2 s
• 10 stops: 1/125 s becomes 8 s

How to use one
• Compose and focus without the filter
• Switch to manual focus so it does not hunt
• Note the shutter speed, fit the filter, and work out the new time
• Cover the viewfinder on long exposures to stop light leaking in

Which strength do you use most: 3, 6 or 10 stops? Tell me in the comments.

trust-the-histogram.caption:
Trust the histogram, not the screen

Why the screen lies
Camera screens are bright, and look brighter still at dawn or at night. A photo that looks fine there can be far too dark at home.

Reading the histogram
• Left side: shadows. Right side: highlights
• A tall spike against the right edge means lost highlights
• Turn on the highlight warning so clipped areas flash

A good habit
Expose as bright as you can without the important highlights flashing. Bright skies at sunrise are the usual problem.

challenge-blue-hour.caption:
Blue hour on your doorstep

The rules
• Go out just after sunset, somewhere near home
• Find lit windows, street lights or a bridge
• Shoot while the sky is still deep blue, not black

Starting settings
• Tripod, lowest ISO, f/8
• Shutter speeds of a few seconds
• White balance on daylight, or adjust it later from RAW

Timing
Blue hour starts soon after sunset and usually lasts 20 to 40 minutes, longer in Scotland in winter. The best moment is when the sky matches the brightness of the lights.

into-the-sun-tip.caption:
Shooting straight into the sun

For a sunstar
• Use a small aperture, f/11 to f/16
• Let the sun just peep past an edge: a tree, a hill, a building
• Wide lenses usually give the cleanest stars

Taming flare
• Clean the front of the lens first
• Take off any filter you do not need
• Shade the lens with your hand, just out of frame

Look after your eyes
Never look at the sun through an optical viewfinder, and do not leave the camera pointing at it for long. Use the screen to compose.

Keep every photograph you care about in three copies, each on a different storage point. For example: the computer, an external drive, and one somewhere else entirely.

Why one copy must be away from home
Fire, flood and theft take everything in the house at once. A drive at a relative’s house, or cloud storage, survives that.

Two traps
• A sync folder is not a backup: delete a file and it vanishes everywhere
• A backup you have never restored from is a hope, not a backup

Be honest: how many copies of your photographs do you have right now? Tell me in the comments.

where-to-focus.caption:
Where to focus in a landscape

The old rule
Focus about a third of the way into the scene. It is a fair starting point at f/8 to f/11, but it does not always work with a close foreground.

A better habit
• Focus on the nearest thing that must be sharp, or just behind it
• Take the shot, then zoom in on the screen
• Check the foreground and the far hills
• Not both sharp? Close down a stop, or take two frames and blend them

high-iso-myth.caption:
High ISO ruins photographs

The truth
This one was taken at ISO 3200. Modern sensors handle high ISO far better than older ones did, and today’s noise reduction is very good.

Blur is worse than noise
A little grain is easy to forgive. A blurred photograph cannot be fixed. If the shutter speed is too slow to hold, raise the ISO.

Keep noise down anyway
• Expose well: lifting dark shadows later shows the most noise
• Use the lowest ISO the light allows
• Reduce noise first, then judge the sharpening

Moving the camera on purpose

Focal length: 24 mm
Aperture: f/22
Shutter: 1/4 s
ISO: 50
Where: Luskentyre, Harris

What ICM is
Intentional camera movement: you move the camera while the shutter is open, turning a scene into lines and colour.

Why these settings
• A slow shutter, around 1/4 s, gives time for the movement
• A small aperture and low ISO keep the shutter slow in daylight
• Strong, simple bands of colour, like sand, sea and sky, work best

How to start
Pan smoothly along the horizon as you press the button. Expect most frames to fail. That is normal.

cleaning-lens.caption:
Cleaning a lens properly

In this order
• Blower first, to lift grit without scratching
• Soft brush for anything left
• Microfibre cloth last, with lens fluid for marks
• Work from the centre outwards

Never
A breath and a shirt sleeve. Sand and salt trapped in fabric can scratch the coating.

Spot dust on the sensor
Photograph a plain sky at f/16. Dark soft spots that sit in the same place on every frame are sensor dust, not the lens.

Lens cloth in the pocket, or something else that gets you through? Tell me in the comments.

street-tips.caption:
Three habits for street photography

Pre-focus
With a 28 to 35 mm lens at f/8, focus manually at about three metres. Everything from about two metres to well past five will be sharp enough, with no waiting for autofocus.

Find the stage first
Look for good light or an interesting background, then wait for someone to walk into it.

Be decent
• Smile if someone notices you
• Delete a photograph if asked
• Think hard before photographing people at their worst

never-edit-myth.caption:
Real photographers don’t edit

The truth
Every digital photograph is processed. A JPEG has been edited by the camera: contrast, colour, sharpening, noise reduction. A RAW file has had none of that yet.

So the choice is
Not whether to edit, but who does it: the camera’s settings or you. Film photographers made the same choices in the darkroom.

Where the line is
Adjusting light and colour is editing. Adding things that were not there is something else, and it is worth being open about.

Where do you draw the line? Tell me in the comments.

waterfall-shutter.caption:
How slow for moving water?

Camera: Canon EOS R5
Focal length: 26 mm
Aperture: f/11
Shutter: 1/2 s
ISO: 200
Where: The Hermitage, Perthshire

A rough guide
• 1/500 s: water frozen in drops
• 1/15 s to 1/2 s: soft, but still with texture
• 2 s and longer: smooth like silk

Things that help
• A tripod, and a two second timer
• A polariser to cut glare on wet rocks
• A cloth for spray, and check the lens between frames

Silky or textured water: which do you prefer? Tell me in the comments.

What it gives you

coast-safety.caption:
No photograph is worth it

On the coast
• Check the tide times and know your way off
• Never turn your back on the sea
• Wet, dark rock is usually slippery

Everywhere
• Tell someone where you are going
• Carry a torch for the walk back after sunset
• Stay on paths: plants and nesting birds come first

stops-explained.caption:
What a stop actually is

One idea
A stop is a doubling or halving of light. Every exposure setting moves in stops.

In practice
• Shutter: 1/250 to 1/125 s is one stop more light
• ISO: 100 to 200 is one stop brighter
• Aperture: f/8 to f/5.6 is one stop more light

Why it matters
Change one setting by a stop, change another by a stop the other way, and the brightness stays the same. That is how you trade sharpness, blur and noise.

What took you longest to understand when you started? Tell me in the comments.

straight-verticals.caption:
Stop buildings falling over

Why they lean
Tilt the camera up and the verticals lean inwards. The building looks as if it is falling backwards.

Fixes
• Keep the camera level and step back
• Use a wider lens and crop away the extra ground
• Correct it afterwards with your editor’s perspective or Upright tools

Or go all in
Point straight up and make the lines dramatic. A small lean looks like a mistake; a big one looks deliberate.

filters-myth.caption:
Editing has replaced filters

Partly true
Graduated filters can often be replaced by taking two exposures and blending them, or by careful editing of a RAW file.

But not these
• A polariser removes glare and reflections: no software can see what is under the surface
• An ND filter gives a long exposure in daylight: editing cannot add real movement

Which filter would you never leave behind? Tell me in the comments.

seascape-waves.caption:
Timing the waves

Shutter speeds
• 1/500 s or faster to freeze a breaking wave
• 1/4 s to 1 s for trails as water pulls back
• Several seconds for a smooth, misty sea

Timing
Watch a few waves first. Press as a wave starts to run back down the rocks or sand: that is when the best trails form.

Keep the lens clean
Salt spray softens everything. Check and wipe the front of the lens often.
